items.title: Rod Stewart Cancels Upcoming Tour Dates Following Coronary Stent Procedure
items.summary:
Rod Stewart has canceled four weeks of concerts after undergoing a coronary stent procedure, wiping out dates on his One Last Time farewell tour and pausing his Encore Shows residency in Las Vegas. A representative for the 81-year-old singer said doctors are satisfied with his recovery and that he has resumed normal daily activities, but needs time off before returning to the stage.

"I'm already feeling better and very much on the mend," Stewart said in a statement. "I want to thank the doctors, nurses and everyone who has taken such wonderful care of me. I'm deeply disappointed to miss these shows and sorry to let my fans down, but I look forward to getting back on stage and having a good time with you all again soon."

The cancellation follows a last-minute postponement of a show at Riverbend Music Center in Cincinnati, which Stewart's camp attributed at the time to a minor medical procedure. According to Variety, the affected shows include a performance at Cleveland's Rocket Arena, which the venue announced was canceled a day earlier, and a Saturday date at Kansas City's Morton Amphitheater.

Stewart had been scheduled to return to the Colosseum at Caesars Palace on Aug. 18 for a run of Las Vegas shows through the end of the month, then continue on to dates in Minnesota, Illinois and Mexico. He has been touring behind One Last Time with Richard Marx since 2024.

This is not the first stretch of scrapped performances this year. Stewart canceled two Las Vegas shows in early June on his doctor's advice, dropped a San Diego date shortly before he was due onstage later that month, and paused a subsequent Utah concert to use an oxygen tank backstage.

Stewart's representatives said venues and promoters will handle information about the canceled performances directly with ticket holders.

items.title: Steve Lacy Is Bringing ‘Oh Yeah?’ on the Road With North American Tour
items.summary:
Steve Lacy has scheduled a 27-date North American tour behind his third studio album, Oh Yeah?, released earlier this year. The run opens Sept. 27 at The Armory in Minneapolis and closes Nov. 30 at the Doug Mitchell Thunderbird Sports Centre in Vancouver.

The itinerary includes Radio City Music Hall in New York on Oct. 10 and the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles on Nov. 21, along with stops in Chicago, Toronto, Laval, Boston, Washington, D.C., Virginia Beach, Charlotte, Miami, Atlanta, Nashville, Austin, Houston, Las Vegas, Phoenix, San Diego, San Francisco and Seattle. Lacy will also play Red Rocks Amphitheatre in Morrison, Colorado, on Nov. 11. General ticket sales begin Friday, Aug. 14, at 10 a.m. local time.

The tour is Lacy's first headlining run in four years, arriving after the period when his profile expanded sharply through viral streaming success. Speaking to Rolling Stone in 2025 about that first stretch on the road, he described the adjustment as jarring. "It was a culture shock for me because I was so used to being niche, a cool music-nerd person," he said.

Lacy said the crowds that came with that attention took some getting used to. "I think going on the road post-Covid and going viral at the same time invited a lot of rambunctious kids who are going to concerts for the first time. So at first, my body rejected it," he said, adding that he came around by the end of the run: "I'm showing them how to be at a concert, so I want to embrace that energy myself."

Oh Yeah? follows Lacy's earlier solo work and collects songs built around escalating degrees of connection. The fall dates give the album its first sustained live presentation.

items.title: Denzel Curry & Kenneth Blume Announce New Album ii: Hear “Difference” (Feat. Yebba)
items.summary:
Denzel Curry and producer Kenneth Blume, the artist formerly billed as Kenny Beats, will release a new collaborative album called ii in nine days. The pair shared the lead single "Difference," featuring vocals from Yebba, along with a video directed by NOTACHANCE that splits the screen between Curry and Blume beginning their respective days in crackly VHS-style footage.

The record is the sequel of sorts to Unlocked, the compact 2020 collaboration the two recorded in a three-day session that grew out of Curry's appearance on Blume's YouTube series The Cave. Blume has since expanded his production credits to include Geese and Weezer, and he reunited with another old collaborator, Rico Nasty, on the album RX a few weeks ago.

Stereogum reported that, per a press release, the making of ii involved significant friction between the two, and that they ultimately stripped the process down to an SP-404 sampler and an inexpensive microphone. "The work Denzel and I do has never been easy, which is why it's so rewarding," Blume said in the promotional materials. "We've started every project on opposite sides of a coin and fought our way to the center. When I hear this album, I hear the growth and the fight in equal parts."

"Difference" lands as a dense, fast-moving boom-bap track with Curry rapping in sharp, animated form over Yebba's hook. Elsewhere on the album, Westside Gunn appears on "Crown" and JPEGMAFIA turns up on "Evil Grin." The nine-track sequence also includes "Gone Fishing," "Candlelight," "Product," "UPS," "Benjamin" and "Cold Night In Hell."

The album arrives during a busy stretch for Curry, who earlier this year introduced his rap group the Scythe and released the crew album Strictly 4 The Scythe. He is also preparing to tour with Knocked Loose and has spoken about moving toward hardcore, a direction Blume, who has produced for Show Me The Body and Trash Talk, could plausibly support.

items.title: Kennedy Center Ordered to Pay $250,000 to Jazz Musician It Unsuccessfully Sued for Backing Out of Concert After Trump Rebranding
items.summary:
A District of Columbia judge has ordered the Kennedy Center to pay jazz musician Chuck Redd $252,000 in legal fees and costs, the final chapter in a breach-of-contract suit the institution filed against him and lost. Redd had withdrawn from the center's annual Christmas Eve concert last December, citing what he called the defiant and illegal name change that temporarily added Donald Trump's name to the organization.

Redd had hosted and performed at the Christmas Eve concerts for years. After he pulled out, Richard Grenell, then the center's president, sent him a letter stating, "This is your official notice that we will seek $1 million in damages from you for this political stunt." The center followed through and sued.

D.C. Superior Court Judge Tanya Jones Bosier dismissed the case in June, finding there was nothing to breach. "I could not find a valid breach-of-contract claim here," she said. "There's no dispute that he did not sign the 2025 agreement." The Kennedy Center had argued Redd was bound to a $6,500 written contract whether or not he signed it.

According to Variety, Redd's attorneys said the center quietly offered to settle before the dismissal, proposing to drop the suit if Redd paid $7,500 and performed on Christmas Eve 2026 without political commentary or discussion of why he withdrew in 2025. Attorney Lisa J. Banks said in a statement Tuesday that "no citizen should have to spend time and money fending off baseless and politically motivated lawsuits filed by the Trump Administration."

The center's lawyers had called the requested fee amount "out of all proportion to the issue at stake," but Jones Bosier concluded $252,000 was reasonable given the work Redd's legal team performed. A separate federal ruling on May 29 found the board's move to add Trump's name to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts was illegal and ordered its removal.

The facade remains under a tarp after workers pried the lettering off, and a judge has asked the board to explain why the covering has not come down.

items.title: Lakers to Be Sold to Bob Iger and Joshua Kushner’s Firm
items.summary:
The Los Angeles Lakers are changing hands again, less than a year after their last sale. Former Disney chief executive Bob Iger and investor Joshua Kushner are set to take over the franchise in a deal that few in the sports business world saw coming.

Kushner's Thrive Capital had been examining major sports acquisitions in recent months, according to a financial-world source cited by The Hollywood Reporter, but the Lakers were widely assumed not to be available. In a joint statement to ESPN, Kushner and Iger said, "As lifelong NBA fans, we are deeply honored for the opportunity to become stewards of the Los Angeles Lakers, one of the most iconic sports franchises in the world." They added that their "long-term commitment is to build on that foundation, compete at the highest level, and serve this extraordinary team, its fans, and the city of Los Angeles."

The sale ends an unusually brief tenure for Mark Walter, the financier who bought the team from the Buss family after more than 45 years of their ownership. The NBA Board of Governors approved Walter's purchase in October. "I am grateful to Jeanie Buss, the Buss family, the players, and the staff for welcoming me into this chapter," Walter told ESPN. "The Lakers belong to Los Angeles, and I have every confidence the best is still ahead."

Walter's arrival had been received warmly in Los Angeles, given his controlling stakes in the Dodgers, the WNBA's Sparks and Chelsea F.C., and the Dodgers' back-to-back World Series titles. His broader business has since drawn regulatory attention. In July, The Wall Street Journal reported that the U.S. Attorney's Office in Manhattan and the Securities and Exchange Commission were examining roughly $16 billion in loans made by his asset-management firm, Guggenheim Investments, for potential fraud.

Iger and Kushner's statement singled out Jerry and Jeanie Buss, whose family oversaw the Showtime era and the Shaquille O'Neal and Kobe Bryant championship years. The deal marks the second ownership transition for the franchise in under twelve months.
